lessons.title: The turning sky

blocks.text: The pole stays put

Earth spins about an axis that points at two fixed spots on the sky, the celestial poles, so every star seems to wheel around them. Seen from latitude φ, the raised pole stands exactly φ degrees above the horizon. From Amsterdam at 52° N it is 52° up; on the equator it sits on the horizon; at the North Pole it is overhead. Polaris lies within a degree of the north celestial pole, which is how sailors read their latitude from it.
Fifteen degrees an hour

Stars complete one circle in 23 hours 56 minutes, the sidereal day. For a night's observing, 360° in 24 hours, or 15° per hour, is close enough. Six hours carries a star a quarter of the way around its daily circle, from rising in the east to crossing the meridian for a star on the celestial equator.
Stars that never set

A star stays up all night when even the lowest point of its circle is above the horizon. That lowest point lies 90° − δ below the pole, and the pole stands φ above the horizon, so the star never sets when δ > 90° − φ. From 52° N every star north of declination +38° is circumpolar; from 10° N only stars beyond +80° qualify.
Highest on the meridian

Each star climbs highest as it crosses the meridian, the north–south line through the zenith. Its altitude then is 90° − |φ − δ|. A star at +20° seen from 52° N culminates 58° above the southern horizon. Southern latitudes and declinations take negative signs, and the same rule works unchanged.

lessons.orientation: Use latitude and declination to predict where a star climbs, and whether it ever sets.

lessons.title: Why the seasons change

blocks.text: A tilted axis that keeps its direction

Earth's axis is tilted 23.4° from upright to its orbit and keeps pointing the same way in space. Around 21 June the northern hemisphere leans towards the Sun and the Sun's declination reaches +23.4°; around 21 December it reaches −23.4°. The noon Sun stands at 90° − |φ − δ|. In London, at 51.5° N, that is 90 − 28.1 = 61.9° in June.
Low sunlight spreads thin

In December the London noon Sun climbs only 90 − 74.9 = 15.1°. A beam arriving at altitude h covers 1/sin h times the ground it would cover from overhead: 3.8 times at 15.1° against 1.13 times at 61.9°. Days are shorter too, about 7.6 hours of daylight in December against 16.4 hours in June, so the ground gains far less energy.
Equinoxes

At the March and September equinoxes the Sun sits on the celestial equator, declination 0°. Day and night are then close to 12 hours everywhere, and the noon Sun stands at 90° − φ. From 40° N that is 50°; from the equator the Sun passes straight overhead.
If the tilt changed

With no tilt, the Sun's declination would stay at 0° and London's noon Sun would sit at 38.5° all year: no seasons from geometry. A 40° tilt would swing it between 78.5° and −1.5°, below the horizon at midwinter noon. Distance plays little part: Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, and its distance varies by only about 3%.

lessons.title: Phases and eclipses

blocks.text: Always half lit

Sunlight always lights one half of the Moon. The phase records how much of that lit half faces Earth. If θ is the angle between Sun and Moon as seen from Earth, the lit fraction of the disc is (1 − cos θ)/2: zero at new moon, one half at θ = 90°, and the whole disc at full moon, when θ = 180°.
A 29.5-day cycle

From one new moon to the next takes 29.53 days, the synodic month. In that time the Moon gains a full 360° on the Sun, about 12.2° a day, so it rises roughly 50 minutes later each night. First quarter comes 7.38 days after new moon and stands highest around sunset; full moon rises as the Sun sets.
Why not every month

The Moon's orbit is tilted 5.1° to the ecliptic, the plane of Earth's orbit. Most full moons pass north or south of Earth's shadow, and most new moons cast their shadow above or below Earth. A lunar eclipse needs a full moon close to the ecliptic, within about 1° in this model, so that the Moon passes through Earth's shadow.
The same size in the sky

For small angles, angular size in radians is diameter divided by distance; multiply by 57.3 for degrees. The Moon, 3,475 km across at 384,400 km, spans 0.52°. The Sun, 400 times wider and about 390 times farther, spans 0.53°. That near match lets a new moon on the ecliptic just cover the Sun's bright disc in a total solar eclipse.

lessons.title: Kepler's laws

blocks.text: Ellipses with the Sun at a focus

Kepler's first law: each planet moves on an ellipse with the Sun at one focus. The semi-major axis a is half the longest diameter, and the eccentricity e says how far the focus sits from the centre, as a fraction of a. Closest approach, perihelion, is a(1 − e); the farthest point, aphelion, is a(1 + e). For a = 2 AU and e = 0.6 those are 0.8 AU and 3.2 AU. Earth's e is 0.017, so its distance changes by about 3%.
Equal areas in equal times

Kepler's second law: the line from Sun to planet sweeps equal areas in equal times. Near the Sun that line is short, so the planet must cover a longer arc in the same time and moves faster. The speeds at the two ends of the long axis are in the inverse ratio of the distances: for a = 2 AU and e = 0.6 the planet is 3.2/0.8 = 4 times faster at perihelion than at aphelion.
Bigger orbits take longer

Kepler's third law: the square of the period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis. With P in years and a in AU around the Sun, P² = a³. An orbit with a = 4 AU has P² = 64, so P = 8 years. The period depends only on a, not on how stretched the ellipse is.
Around a heavier star

Newton showed why the third law holds and what sets its constant. Around a star of M solar masses the law becomes P² = a³/M. A planet 1 AU from a 4-solar-mass star has P² = 1/4, a period of half a year: a stronger pull needs a faster orbit to keep from falling inward.

lessons.title: Newton's gravitation

blocks.text: The inverse square

Newton's law of gravitation: F = GMm/r², with G = 6.674 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg². Double the separation and the force falls to a quarter; triple it and the force falls to a ninth, 0.111 of its first value. The arrows in the drawing share one scale, so you can watch them shrink.
Both masses count

The force is proportional to the product of the masses. Doubling one mass and tripling the other multiplies the force by 2 × 3 = 6 at the same separation. A body's own mass does not let it escape the pull: twice the mass means twice the force.
Surface gravity from G, M and R

Divide the force on a mass m by m and the field at distance r is g = GM/r². For Earth, GM = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s² and R = 6,371 km, so g = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ / (6.371 × 10⁶)² = 9.82 m/s². Every falling object gets this acceleration whatever its own mass, which is why a hammer and a feather fall together on the airless Moon.
Equal and opposite

The same formula gives the pull of Earth on the Moon and of the Moon on Earth: GMm/r² does not care which body you call M. The forces are equal in size and opposite in direction. Earth has 81 times the Moon's mass, so the same force gives Earth one eighty-first of the Moon's acceleration.

lessons.title: Orbits, escape and tides

blocks.text: Falling around the planet

An orbit is a fall that keeps missing. At distance r from the centre, a horizontal speed v = √(GM/r) curves away from a straight line exactly as fast as gravity pulls inward, so the path closes into a circle. At 400 km up, r = 6,771 km and v = 7.67 km/s. Slower, the path dips into the atmosphere and the ground; faster, it stretches into an ellipse.
Escape speed

Launch fast enough and the path opens out and never returns. That escape speed is v = √(2GM/r), always √2 = 1.414 times the circular speed at the same distance. From Earth's surface it is √(2 × 3.986 × 10¹⁴ / 6.371 × 10⁶) = 11.19 km/s, ignoring air resistance.
Earth around the Sun

The same formula works for planets around the Sun. With GM☉ = 1.327 × 10²⁰ m³/s² and r = 1 AU = 1.496 × 10¹¹ m, Earth's orbital speed is √(GM/r) = 29.8 km/s, matching NASA's measured mean of 29.78 km/s. Jupiter, 5.2 times farther out, moves √5.2 = 2.3 times more slowly.
Tides from a difference in pull

The Moon pulls the near ocean harder than Earth's centre, and Earth's centre harder than the far ocean, so the oceans stretch into two bulges and a coast sees two high tides a day. Because it is a difference in pull, the stretch falls as the cube of distance: halve the Moon's distance and its tides grow 2³ = 8 times. The Sun's tide is 0.46 of the Moon's; aligned at new and full moon they add to make spring tides.

lessons.title: Brightness and distance

blocks.text: Light spreads over a sphere

A star's luminosity L, its total power output, spreads over a sphere of area 4πd² at distance d. The flux F = L/(4πd²) is the power arriving on each square metre. At twice the distance the same light covers four times the area, so the flux drops to a quarter; at three times, to a ninth.
Sunlight at Earth

The Sun's luminosity is 3.828 × 10²⁶ W. At 1 AU, 1.496 × 10¹¹ m, that power is shared over 4π(1.496 × 10¹¹)² = 2.812 × 10²³ m², giving 1,361 W on every square metre facing the Sun above the atmosphere. Mars, at 1.52 AU, receives 1/1.52² = 0.43 of that.
Parallax measures distance

As Earth swings around the Sun, a nearby star shifts against far more distant stars. Half that seasonal shift, measured from a baseline of 1 AU, is the parallax p. A star with p = 1 arcsecond is by definition 1 parsec away, 206,265 AU or 3.26 light-years, and in general d = 1/p parsecs. Proxima Centauri, with p = 0.768″, is 1.30 pc away.
Bright because close, or bright because powerful

Apparent brightness alone cannot separate a powerful distant star from a feeble nearby one. Flux is proportional to L/d², so a star 100 times more luminous looks equally bright from √100 = 10 times farther away. Once parallax gives d, the measured flux gives the luminosity: L = 4πd²F.

lessons.title: Temperature, colour and motion

blocks.text: Hotter glows bluer

A star radiates roughly like a blackbody, whose spectrum has one peak. Wien's law places it at λmax = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K / T. The Sun's 5,772 K surface peaks at 502 nm, in the blue-green, but emits across the visible so it looks white. A 3,500 K star peaks in the infrared and looks orange-red; a 20,000 K star peaks in the ultraviolet and looks blue-white.
Temperature from the peak

Run Wien's law backwards to take a star's temperature from a distance: T = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K / λmax. A spectrum peaking at 290 nm means T = 2.898 × 10⁻³ / 2.90 × 10⁻⁷ = 9,990 K, close to 10,000 K, like Vega. Hotter objects are also far brighter per square metre: the emitted flux grows as T⁴.
Lines shift with motion

Atoms absorb and emit at fixed wavelengths, measured in the laboratory. A source moving away stretches its waves to longer wavelengths, a redshift; one approaching shortens them, a blueshift. For speeds well below light's, v = cΔλ/λ. Hydrogen's 656.28 nm line seen at 662.84 nm shifts by 6.56 nm, so the source recedes at 3.00 × 10⁵ × 6.56/656.28 = 3,000 km/s.
Small speeds, small shifts

Stars in our galaxy move at tens to hundreds of kilometres per second, so their shifts are a fraction of a nanometre and need a good spectrograph. A star approaching at 150 km/s shifts a 500.00 nm line by 500 × 150/300,000 = 0.25 nm towards the blue. Only the motion along the line of sight shows up; sideways motion produces no first-order shift.

lessons.orientation: Read a star's temperature from its colour and its motion from shifted spectral lines.

lessons.title: The H–R diagram

blocks.text: Luminosity from size and temperature

Each square metre of a star's surface emits σT⁴, and the surface has area 4πR². So L = 4πR²σT⁴, or in solar units L = R²(T/5,772 K)⁴. A star of the Sun's size at twice its temperature emits 2⁴ = 16 times as much. Temperature is a powerful lever.
Big and cool

Plot luminosity against temperature with hot stars on the left, and the stars fall into groups. Most lie on the main sequence, the diagonal band. Up and to the right sit cool stars so luminous they must be enormous. A 3,600 K red supergiant 760 times the Sun's radius has L = 760² × (3,600/5,772)⁴ = 87,000 L☉.
Small and hot

Down in the lower left lie white dwarfs: hot but dim, so they must be tiny. One of radius 0.01 R☉ (about Earth's size) at four times the Sun's temperature has L = 0.01² × 4⁴ = 0.0256 L☉. The dashed lines on the diagram mark constant radius.
Reading the diagram

Two stars at the same temperature emit the same power per square metre, so a difference in luminosity must come from surface area. A star 100 times more luminous than another of equal temperature has √100 = 10 times its radius. Height on the diagram at a fixed temperature is a measure of size.

lessons.title: How mass sets a star's life

blocks.text: More fuel, burned much faster

A star spends most of its life on the main sequence, fusing hydrogen in its core. A heavier star has more fuel, roughly in proportion to its mass M, but its core is hotter and denser, so it shines roughly as M³·⁵. Lifetime is fuel divided by burn rate, so t ∝ M/M³·⁵ = M⁻²·⁵. Scaled to the Sun's 10 billion years, a 4 M☉ star lasts 10 × 4⁻²·⁵ = 0.3125 billion years: 312.5 million.
Luminosity climbs steeply

The rule L ∝ M³·⁵ is a fit to measured main-sequence stars, good to a factor of about two between half and twenty solar masses. A 2 M☉ star shines at 2³·⁵ = 11.3 L☉; a 10 M☉ star at about 3,200 L☉. Mass is the single number that fixes a main-sequence star's place on the H–R diagram.
Small stars outlast the universe

Low-mass stars burn so slowly that the rule gives a 0.5 M☉ red dwarf 10 × 0.5⁻²·⁵ = 56.6 billion years, four times the present age of the universe. No red dwarf has yet left the main sequence. The OpenStax table lists 200 billion years for 0.4 M☉; the power law is an estimate, not a precise clock.
Mass decides the ending

When core hydrogen runs out, the core contracts and the outer layers swell into a giant. Following the OpenStax table of end states: stars that begin below about 10 M☉ shed their envelopes and leave white dwarfs; those of about 10 to 40 M☉ explode as supernovae and leave neutron stars; heavier ones leave black holes. The boundaries are uncertain and depend on how much mass a star loses.

lessons.title: Galaxies and Hubble's law

blocks.text: A universe of galaxies

The Milky Way is a disc of a few hundred billion stars about 100,000 light-years across, one galaxy among billions. Distances between galaxies are measured in megaparsecs: 1 Mpc = 3.26 million light-years. The Andromeda galaxy, about 0.78 Mpc away, is seen by light that left it 0.78 × 3.26 = 2.5 million years ago.
Velocity grows with distance

Galaxy spectra are redshifted, and the redshift grows with distance. Hubble's law states it as v = H₀d. Measurements of H₀ cluster around 70 km/s per megaparsec, so a galaxy 100 Mpc away recedes at 7,000 km/s and one at 200 Mpc at 14,000 km/s.
Everyone sees the same

Play the expansion and every spacing on the grid grows by the same factor. A galaxy twice as far gains twice the distance in the same time, so every observer, in any galaxy, sees others receding at speeds proportional to their distance. The pattern needs no centre. Reversing the law, a recession speed gives a distance: d = v/H₀.
An uncertain constant

Different methods give H₀ between about 67 and 73 km/s/Mpc, a disagreement astronomers call the Hubble tension. For a galaxy 300 Mpc away the two values predict speeds of 20,100 and 21,900 km/s, a difference of 6 × 300 = 1,800 km/s. Distances inferred from velocities inherit the same uncertainty.

lessons.title: The age and afterglow of the Big Bang

blocks.text: Run the expansion backwards

If every galaxy had always receded at its present speed, a galaxy at distance d would have set off a time d/v = d/(H₀d) = 1/H₀ ago, the same for all of them. With H₀ = 70 km/s/Mpc, 1/H₀ = 3.086 × 10¹⁹ km ÷ 70 km/s = 4.41 × 10¹⁷ s, about 14.0 billion years. Careful modelling of the changing expansion gives 13.8 billion years.
A glow from every direction

In 1965 Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson found faint microwave radiation coming equally from every direction. Its spectrum is an almost perfect blackbody at 2.725 K, peaking at 2.898 × 10⁻³ / 2.725 = 1.06 × 10⁻³ m, about 1.06 mm. A cold, uniform glow filling space is what a universe that was once hot and dense should leave behind.
Stretched by expansion

About 380,000 years after the Big Bang the universe had cooled to about 3,000 K, cool enough for electrons to join nuclei into neutral atoms. Light then travelled freely. Since then expansion has stretched every wavelength, and a blackbody's temperature falls in the same proportion, so 3,000/2.725 = 1,100 is the stretch factor.
How much the constant matters

The age estimate is inversely proportional to H₀. A smaller H₀ means slower expansion and an older universe: H₀ = 50 km/s/Mpc gives 1/H₀ = 19.6 billion years. Stars older than 1/H₀ would be a contradiction, which is one reason astronomers check stellar ages against the expansion age.

questions.prompt: From latitude 52° N, what is the altitude of the north celestial pole, in degrees?
hints: The pole's altitude is tied to where you stand on Earth.
At the equator the pole is on the horizon; at the North Pole it is overhead.
Altitude of the pole equals the observer's latitude.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The raised celestial pole stands at an altitude equal to the latitude: 52°.

questions.prompt: The sky turns at about 15° per hour. Through what angle, in degrees, does a star move around its daily circle in 6 hours?
hints: The rate is constant through the night.
Multiply the rate by the time.
Calculate 15 × 6.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 15° per hour × 6 h = 90°, a quarter of a full circle.

questions.prompt: From latitude 52° N, a star is circumpolar when its declination exceeds 90° − φ. What is that smallest declination, in degrees?
hints: The lowest point of the star's circle must stay above the horizon.
The lowest point lies 90° − δ below a pole that is φ high.
Subtract the latitude from 90°.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: δ > 90° − 52° = 38°. Stars north of +38° never set from 52° N.

hints: The star's circle stays around the pole without dipping below the horizon.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Circumpolar: its whole daily circle stays above the horizon around the celestial pole.

questions.prompt: London lies at 51.5° N. Taking Earth's tilt as 23.4°, find the Sun's noon altitude at the June solstice, in degrees, to one decimal place.
hints: At the June solstice the Sun's declination equals the tilt, north of the equator.
Find 51.5 − 23.4 first, then subtract it from 90.

questions.prompt: Find the Sun's noon altitude in London (51.5° N) at the December solstice, with a tilt of 23.4°, to one decimal place.
hints: In December the Sun's declination is south of the equator, so it is negative.
Subtract that sum from 90°.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: At the December solstice δ = −23.4°. Altitude = 90° − |51.5° + 23.4°| = 90° − 74.9° = 15.1°.

questions.prompt: At an equinox the Sun's declination is 0°. Find the noon altitude of the Sun from latitude 40° N, in degrees.
hints: Set δ to zero.
The rule reduces to 90° − φ.
Subtract the latitude from 90°.

questions.prompt: Imagine Earth had no axial tilt. What would the Sun's noon altitude be in London (51.5° N) on every date, in degrees, to one decimal place?
hints: Without tilt the Sun never leaves the celestial equator.
Its declination is zero on every date.
Subtract the latitude from 90°.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: With no tilt δ = 0° all year, so the noon altitude is always 90° − 51.5° = 38.5°.

questions.prompt: At what northern latitude, in degrees, is the noon Sun directly overhead at the June solstice, taking Earth's tilt as 23.4°? Give one decimal place.
hints: Directly overhead means an altitude of 90°.
Set 90° − |φ − δ| equal to 90°.
The latitude must match the Sun's declination on that date.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Overhead means altitude 90°, so |φ − δ| = 0 and φ = δ = 23.4° N, the Tropic of Cancer.

hints: Divide a³ by the star's mass in solar masses.
1 cubed is 1.
Take the square root of a quarter.

questions.prompt: Jupiter's orbital period is 11.86 years. Using P² = a³, find its semi-major axis in AU, to two decimal places.
hints: Square the period to get a³.
11.86² is about 140.7.
Take the cube root of that.

questions.prompt: What name is given to the point of a planet's orbit closest to the Sun?
hints: It begins with the Greek prefix for 'near'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Perihelion, from Greek peri (near) and helios (Sun). The farthest point is aphelion.

questions.prompt: Two bodies are moved from separation r to 3r. By what factor does the gravitational force between them change? Give three decimal places.
hints: Gravity follows an inverse-square law.
Square the factor by which the distance grew.
Take the reciprocal of 3².

questions.prompt: At a fixed separation, one mass is doubled and the other tripled. By what factor does the gravitational force change?
hints: The force is proportional to the product of the masses.
Each mass change multiplies the force.
Multiply the two factors.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: F ∝ Mm, so the force changes by 2 × 3 = 6.

questions.prompt: Earth's GM is 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s² and its radius is 6,371 km. Find g = GM/R² at the surface, in m/s², to two decimal places.
hints: Convert the radius to metres first.
Square 6.371 × 10⁶ m.
Divide GM by that square.

questions.prompt: Earth has 81 times the Moon's mass. Find the ratio of the force Earth exerts on the Moon to the force the Moon exerts on Earth.
hints: Write the force on each body with Newton's law.
The two expressions contain the same masses and distance.
Compare GMm/r² with GmM/r².

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Both forces equal GMm/r², so the ratio is exactly one: equal and opposite.

questions.prompt: Mars has GM = 4.283 × 10¹³ m³/s² and radius 3,390 km. Find its surface gravity in m/s², to two decimal places.
hints: Use g = GM/R² with R in metres.
Square 3.39 × 10⁶.
Divide GM by that square.

questions.prompt: Why do a hammer and a feather dropped together on the Moon land together?
hints: Divide the gravitational force by the falling object's own mass.

acceptedIdeas: The pull on each is proportional to its mass, so the acceleration GM/r² is the same for both
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Force GMm/r² divided by the object's mass m leaves GM/r², the same for any object at that place. With no air there is no drag to separate them.

choices.label: The pull on each is proportional to its mass, so the acceleration GM/r² is the same for both
The Moon's gravity does not act on light objects
Heavier objects are pulled less strongly per kilogram

questions.prompt: Find the circular orbital speed 400 km above Earth, where r = 6,771 km and GM = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s², in km/s, to two decimal places.
hints: Use v = √(GM/r) with r in metres.
Divide GM by 6.771 × 10⁶ m.
Take the square root and convert from m/s to km/s.

questions.prompt: Find the escape speed from Earth's surface, with R = 6,371 km and GM = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s², in km/s, to two decimal places.
hints: Use v = √(2GM/r).
Double GM, then divide by the radius in metres.
Take the square root and convert to km/s.

questions.prompt: Using v = √(GM/r) with GM☉ = 1.327 × 10²⁰ m³/s² and r = 1.496 × 10¹¹ m, find Earth's orbital speed in km/s, to one decimal place.
hints: This is a circular-orbit speed around the Sun.
Divide GM☉ by the distance in metres.
Take the square root, then divide by 1,000.

questions.prompt: Tidal stretching falls as the cube of distance. If the Moon were at half its present distance, by what factor would its tides grow?
hints: A tide is a difference in pull across Earth.
That difference scales as one over distance cubed.
Cube the factor of 2.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Tide ∝ 1/d³, so halving d multiplies the tide by 2³ = 8.

questions.prompt: The Moon has GM = 4.90 × 10¹² m³/s² and radius 1,737 km. Find the escape speed from its surface in km/s, to two decimal places.
hints: Escape speed is √(2GM/R).
Convert the radius to metres.
Compute the square root and convert to km/s.

questions.prompt: Why are the tides largest around new moon and full moon?
hints: Think about where the Sun lies relative to the Earth–Moon line at those phases.

acceptedIdeas: The Sun's and the Moon's tidal stretches line up and add
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: At new and full moon the Sun, Earth and Moon are in line, so the solar tide (0.46 of the lunar tide) adds to the Moon's: spring tides. At the quarters they partly cancel: neap tides.

choices.label: The Sun's and the Moon's tidal stretches line up and add
The Moon is always closest to Earth at those phases
Earth spins faster at those phases

questions.prompt: A probe moves from 1 AU to 2 AU from the Sun. What fraction of the solar flux it received at 1 AU does it now receive?
hints: Light spreads over a sphere of area 4πd².
Doubling d multiplies that area by 2².
Take the reciprocal of 2².

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Flux ∝ 1/d², so it falls to 1/2² = 1/4 = 0.25 of its value at 1 AU.

questions.prompt: The Sun's luminosity is 3.828 × 10²⁶ W. Find the flux at 1 AU = 1.496 × 10¹¹ m, in W/m², to the nearest whole number.
hints: Use F = L/(4πd²).
Square the distance in metres, then multiply by 4π.
Divide the luminosity by that area.

questions.prompt: Proxima Centauri's parallax is 0.768 arcseconds. Find its distance in parsecs, to two decimal places.
hints: Distance in parsecs is the reciprocal of parallax in arcseconds.
Divide 1 by the parallax.
Round to two decimal places.

questions.prompt: Star A is 100 times as luminous as star B, yet they appear equally bright. How many times farther away than B is A?
hints: Flux is proportional to L/d².
Keep the flux fixed while L grows a hundredfold.
Then d² must grow by the same factor; take the square root.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Equal flux needs L/d² equal, so d grows as √L: √100 = 10 times farther.

questions.prompt: A star's parallax is 0.05 arcseconds. Find its distance in light-years, to one decimal place, using 1 pc = 3.26 ly.
hints: First convert parallax to parsecs with d = 1/p.
Then multiply by 3.26 light-years per parsec.

questions.prompt: What unit of distance is defined as the distance at which a star shows a parallax of one arcsecond?
hints: Its name joins the first syllables of the two words that define it.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The parsec: PARallax of one arcSECond. It equals 206,265 AU or 3.26 light-years.

questions.prompt: Using Wien's law λmax = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K / T, find the peak wavelength of the Sun (T = 5,772 K) in nanometres, to the nearest whole number.
hints: Divide Wien's constant by the temperature.
The result comes out in metres.
Multiply by 10⁹ to convert metres to nanometres.

questions.prompt: A star's spectrum peaks at 290 nm. Find its surface temperature in kelvin, to the nearest hundred.
hints: Rearrange Wien's law for T.
Write the peak wavelength in metres.
Divide the constant by that wavelength, then round.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: T = 2.898 × 10⁻³ / 2.90 × 10⁻⁷ = 9,993 K, which is 10,000 K to the nearest hundred.

questions.prompt: A hydrogen line with laboratory wavelength 656.28 nm is observed at 662.84 nm. Using v = cΔλ/λ with c = 3.00 × 10⁵ km/s, find the radial velocity in km/s, to the nearest ten (positive means receding).
hints: Find the shift: observed minus laboratory wavelength.
Divide the shift by the laboratory wavelength.
Multiply by the speed of light in km/s.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Δλ = 6.56 nm; v = 3.00 × 10⁵ × 6.56/656.28 = 2,999 km/s, which is 3,000 km/s to the nearest ten, receding.

questions.prompt: A star approaches at 150 km/s. Find the shift of its 500.00 nm line in nanometres, with redshift positive and blueshift negative, to three decimal places. Take c = 3.00 × 10⁵ km/s.
hints: An approaching source has a negative radial velocity.
Use Δλ = λv/c.
Multiply 500 by −150, then divide by 300,000.

questions.prompt: Betelgeuse looks orange-red and Rigel looks blue-white. What does the difference tell you?
hints: Which property of a glowing body sets where its spectrum peaks?

acceptedIdeas: Betelgeuse's surface is cooler, so its spectrum peaks at longer wavelengths
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Colour tracks surface temperature through Wien's law: about 3,600 K for Betelgeuse against about 12,000 K for Rigel. Their radial speeds are far too small to change a colour.

choices.label: Betelgeuse's surface is cooler, so its spectrum peaks at longer wavelengths
Betelgeuse is moving away from us much faster than Rigel
Betelgeuse is farther away, so its light has reddened on the way

questions.prompt: A red dwarf has a surface temperature of 3,000 K. Find its peak wavelength in nanometres, to the nearest whole number.
hints: Use λmax = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K / T.
Divide by 3,000 K.
Convert metres to nanometres.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: λmax = 2.898 × 10⁻³ / 3,000 = 9.66 × 10⁻⁷ m = 966 nm, in the near infrared.

questions.prompt: A star has the Sun's radius but twice the Sun's surface temperature. How many times the Sun's luminosity does it emit?
hints: Use L = R²(T/T☉)⁴ in solar units.
The radius factor is one.
Raise the temperature ratio to the fourth power.

questions.prompt: A red supergiant has a surface temperature of 3,600 K and a radius of 760 R☉. With T☉ = 5,772 K, find its luminosity in solar units, to the nearest thousand.
hints: Square the radius in solar radii.
Raise 3,600/5,772 to the fourth power.
Multiply the two results, then round.

questions.prompt: A white dwarf has radius 0.01 R☉ and a surface temperature four times the Sun's. Find its luminosity in solar units, to four decimal places.
hints: Square the radius.
Raise the temperature factor to the fourth power.
Multiply 0.0001 by 256.

questions.prompt: Two stars have the same surface temperature, but one is far more luminous. Which property of the luminous star must be larger? Answer in one word.
hints: Write L = 4πR²σT⁴ and hold T fixed.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Its radius. Equal temperature means equal power per square metre, so more luminosity needs more surface area.

questions.prompt: Two stars have equal temperatures; one is 100 times as luminous as the other. How many times larger is its radius?
hints: Hold T constant in L ∝ R²T⁴.
Luminosity then scales as radius squared.
Take the square root of the luminosity ratio.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: With T fixed, L ∝ R², so R grows as √100 = 10.

questions.prompt: A star twice the Sun's radius has a luminosity of 4 L☉. Taking T☉ = 5,772 K, find its surface temperature in kelvin.
hints: Write L = R²(T/T☉)⁴ and substitute R = 2.
Divide both sides by R².
Find what temperature ratio raised to the fourth power gives the result.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 4 = 2² × (T/T☉)⁴ gives (T/T☉)⁴ = 1, so T equals the Sun's temperature: 5,772 K.

questions.prompt: Main-sequence lifetime scales as t ≈ 10 billion years × M⁻²·⁵, with M in solar masses. Find the lifetime of a 4 M☉ star in millions of years, to one decimal place.
hints: Raise 4 to the power −2.5.
4²·⁵ is 4² × √4.
Divide 10 billion years by 4²·⁵ and convert to millions.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 4⁻²·⁵ = 1/32, so t = 10 billion/32 = 0.3125 billion years = 312.5 million years.

questions.prompt: Main-sequence luminosity scales roughly as L ∝ M³·⁵. How many times the Sun's luminosity does a 2 M☉ star have? Give one decimal place.
hints: Raise the mass ratio to the power 3.5.
Split 2³·⁵ into 2³ × 2⁰·⁵.
Multiply 8 by √2.

questions.prompt: Using t ≈ 10 billion years × M⁻²·⁵, find the main-sequence lifetime of a 0.5 M☉ red dwarf in billions of years, to one decimal place.
hints: A negative power of one half is a positive power of two.
Work out 2²·⁵.
Multiply by 10 billion years.

questions.prompt: Following the OpenStax table of stellar end states, what remnant does a star of initial mass 15 M☉ leave? Answer in two words.
hints: Its core collapses in a supernova but stops short of a black hole.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A neutron star. Stars of about 10 to 40 M☉ end in a core-collapse supernova that leaves a neutron star.

questions.prompt: A star spends 10 million years on the main sequence. Using t ≈ 10 billion years × M⁻²·⁵, find its mass in solar masses, to the nearest whole number.
hints: Divide the lifetime by 10 billion years to get M⁻²·⁵.
Invert to get M²·⁵.
Raise 1,000 to the power 1/2.5.

questions.prompt: What will the Sun become after its red-giant stage?
hints: Compare the Sun's mass with the boundary for a supernova.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: At 1 M☉ the Sun is well below the 10 M☉ boundary. It will shed its outer layers and leave a carbon-oxygen white dwarf about the size of Earth.

choices.label: A white dwarf
A neutron star
A black hole

questions.prompt: The Andromeda galaxy is about 0.78 Mpc away, and 1 Mpc = 3.26 million light-years. How long ago, in millions of years, did the light we see from it set out? Give one decimal place.
hints: A light-year is the distance light covers in one year.
Convert megaparsecs to millions of light-years.
Multiply 0.78 by 3.26.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 0.78 × 3.26 = 2.54 million light-years, so the light left about 2.5 million years ago.

questions.prompt: With H₀ = 70 km/s per Mpc, find the recession velocity of a galaxy 100 Mpc away, in km/s.
hints: Use Hubble's law v = H₀d.
The units of Mpc cancel.
Multiply 70 by 100.

questions.prompt: A galaxy recedes at 14,000 km/s. With H₀ = 70 km/s per Mpc, how far away is it, in Mpc?
hints: Rearrange v = H₀d for distance.
Divide the velocity by H₀.
Calculate 14,000/70.

questions.prompt: Estimates of H₀ range from 67 to 73 km/s per Mpc. For a galaxy 300 Mpc away, by how many km/s do the two predicted velocities differ?
hints: Compute each velocity with v = H₀d, or work with the difference directly.
The difference in H₀ is 73 − 67.
Multiply that difference by 300 Mpc.

questions.prompt: A galaxy's 500.0 nm line is observed at 510.0 nm. Using v = cΔλ/λ with c = 3.00 × 10⁵ km/s, and H₀ = 70 km/s per Mpc, find its distance in Mpc, to the nearest whole number.
hints: First turn the redshift into a velocity.
Then divide that velocity by H₀.

questions.prompt: Every distant galaxy appears to recede from the Milky Way. What does this tell us about our position?
hints: Imagine standing on a different galaxy on the stretching grid.

acceptedIdeas: Nothing special: uniform expansion gives every galaxy the same view
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: In a uniform expansion all spacings grow by the same factor, so observers in any galaxy see v ∝ d. Recession in every direction does not single out a centre.

choices.label: Nothing special: uniform expansion gives every galaxy the same view
The Milky Way is at the centre of the expansion
The Milky Way is the oldest galaxy

questions.prompt: With H₀ = 70 km/s per Mpc, 1 Mpc = 3.086 × 10¹⁹ km and 1 billion years = 3.156 × 10¹⁶ s, find 1/H₀ in billions of years, to one decimal place.
hints: Write H₀ as 70 km/s per 3.086 × 10¹⁹ km so the kilometres cancel.
Divide 3.086 × 10¹⁹ by 70 to get seconds.
Convert seconds to billions of years.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 1/H₀ = 3.086 × 10¹⁹ km ÷ 70 km/s = 4.409 × 10¹⁷ s; ÷ 3.156 × 10¹⁶ s = 13.97, about 14.0 billion years.

questions.prompt: The cosmic microwave background is a blackbody at 2.725 K. Using λmax = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K / T, find its peak wavelength in millimetres, to two decimal places.
hints: Divide Wien's constant by the temperature.
The result is in metres.
Multiply by 1,000 to convert to millimetres.

questions.prompt: The cosmic background was released at about 3,000 K and is now 2.725 K. By what factor have its wavelengths been stretched since then, to the nearest whole number?
hints: Wien's law makes peak wavelength inversely proportional to temperature.
So the stretch factor is the ratio of the two temperatures.
Divide the earlier temperature by today's.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Temperature falls as wavelengths stretch, so the factor is 3,000/2.725 = 1,100.9, which is 1,101 to the nearest whole number.

questions.prompt: Using 1/H₀ = 977.8 billion years ÷ H₀ (H₀ in km/s per Mpc), find 1/H₀ for H₀ = 50, in billions of years, to one decimal place.
hints: The constant 977.8 converts the units for you.
Divide it by the value of H₀.
Round to one decimal place.

questions.prompt: What kind of spectrum does the cosmic microwave background have? Answer with the one-word name for the spectrum of an ideal thermal emitter.
hints: It is the same kind of spectrum Wien's law describes.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A blackbody spectrum, the closest to perfect ever measured, at 2.725 K.

questions.prompt: Why is 1/H₀ only an approximation to the age of the universe?
hints: What does 1/H₀ assume about each galaxy's speed?

acceptedIdeas: The expansion rate has changed over time, slowed by gravity and later sped up
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 1/H₀ assumes each galaxy kept a constant speed. Gravity slowed the early expansion and dark energy has since accelerated it; the two effects nearly cancel, so 13.8 billion years is close to 1/H₀.

choices.label: The expansion rate has changed over time, slowed by gravity and later sped up
Light from distant galaxies travelled faster than light does now
Galaxies only recede from the Milky Way, so the formula ignores the rest

flashcards.front: From latitude 41° N, how many degrees above the horizon is the north celestial pole?
flashcards.back: The pole's altitude equals the latitude: 41°.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The pole's altitude equals the latitude: 41°.

flashcards.front: At 15° per hour, how many hours does the sky take to turn through 135°?
At latitude 35° N, with Earth's tilt taken as 23.4°, find the Sun's noon altitude at the December solstice, in degrees, to one decimal place.
At latitude 60° N on an equinox, what is the Sun's noon altitude in degrees?
flashcards.back: δ = 0°, so the noon altitude is 90° − 60° = 30°.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: δ = 0°, so the noon altitude is 90° − 60° = 30°.

flashcards.front: What percentage of the Moon's visible disc is lit when the Sun–Earth–Moon angle is 60°?
flashcards.back: (1 − cos 60°)/2 = (1 − 0.5)/2 = 0.25, a quarter of the disc.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: (1 − cos 60°)/2 = (1 − 0.5)/2 = 0.25, a quarter of the disc.

An asteroid has an orbital period of 27 years. Using P² = a³, find its semi-major axis in AU.
An orbit has semi-major axis 5 AU and eccentricity 0.2. Find its aphelion distance in AU.
Two masses are moved from separation r to r/2. By what factor does the gravitational force between them change?
flashcards.back: F ∝ 1/r²; halving r multiplies F by 2² = 4.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: F ∝ 1/r²; halving r multiplies F by 2² = 4.

flashcards.front: Gravity at Earth's surface is 9.82 m/s². Find the field one Earth radius above the surface, in m/s², to three decimal places.
flashcards.back: One radius above the surface is 2R from the centre, so g falls by 2² = 4: 9.82/4 = 2.455 m/s².

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One radius above the surface is 2R from the centre, so g falls by 2² = 4: 9.82/4 = 2.455 m/s².

flashcards.front: Escape speed is how many times the circular orbital speed at the same distance? Give three decimal places.
A satellite circles Earth at r = 42,164 km, where GM = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s². Find its speed in km/s, to two decimal places.
flashcards.back: v = √(3.986 × 10¹⁴ / 4.2164 × 10⁷) = 3,075 m/s, about 3.07 km/s. This is the geostationary orbit.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: v = √(3.986 × 10¹⁴ / 4.2164 × 10⁷) = 3,075 m/s, about 3.07 km/s. This is the geostationary orbit.

Mars orbits 1.52 AU from the Sun. What fraction of the solar flux at Earth reaches Mars? Give two decimal places.
A star's surface temperature is 14,000 K. Using λmax = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K / T, find its peak wavelength in nanometres, to the nearest whole number.

A star has three times the Sun's radius and the Sun's surface temperature. Find its luminosity in solar units.
A star has half the Sun's surface temperature and exactly the Sun's luminosity. Find its radius in solar radii.
flashcards.back: 1 = R² × (1/2)⁴ = R²/16, so R² = 16 and R = 4 R☉.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 1 = R² × (1/2)⁴ = R²/16, so R² = 16 and R = 4 R☉.
